### The Hook: Dr. Chen's Dilemma

Dr. Mei Chen, a postdoc at a top-20 computer science department, stares at two browser tabs open side by side. The first shows the NeurIPS 2025 main track Call for Papers. Its language is unmistakable: the track seeks "new algorithms, theoretical foundations, and novel methods" for machine learning. The second tab shows the NeurIPS 2025 Datasets & Benchmarks track Call for Papers, which asks for something different: "high-quality publications on highly valuable machine learning datasets and benchmarks." Mei has spent the past fourteen months building *both*: a large-scale benchmark of 15,000 hand-annotated multilingual reasoning questions spanning 40 languages, *and* a novel scoring algorithm that correlates better with human judgments than any existing metric. Her benchmark is a substantial research contribution. Her algorithm is algorithmic innovation. The question gnawing at her is deceptively simple: does she write one paper or two?

Her labmate, Aditya, leans over from the next desk. "Just put the benchmark in the appendix of the algorithm paper," he says, tapping the main track CFP. "That's what everyone does. The reviewers want to see that your metric beats the baselines. The benchmark is just the playground." Mei's advisor, Professor Liu, disagrees. She pulls up the NeurIPS 2021 announcement blog post for the Datasets & Benchmarks track and reads aloud: "Work on datasets and benchmarks has been *undervalued, unsupported, and taken for granted*, even though it is crucial for the development and continuous improvement of machine learning methods." She slides her laptop across the table. "Your benchmark is a separate paper. And it might be the more impactful one."

Who is right? The answer requires understanding something that most ML researchers learn too late: the academic publication ecosystem has evolved to recognize different *kinds* of contributions. Forcing a data contribution into an algorithms venue is like submitting a novel to a poetry journal. It might contain beautiful prose, but it will be judged by the wrong criteria. The system is not designed to see its value. This chapter exists to help you see what the system sees, and to write papers that speak its language.

But the stakes are higher than career strategy. Mei's benchmark, if published well, could become the standard evaluation suite for multilingual reasoning. Hundreds of researchers could use it to evaluate their own models, identify weaknesses in particular languages, and track progress over time. If she buries it in an appendix, it will be invisible: a footnote that nobody cites, nobody downloads, and nobody builds on. If she publishes it as a standalone Datasets & Benchmarks paper (with proper documentation, hosted data, baseline experiments, and a clear articulation of what gap it fills), it could shape the research agenda for years. ImageNet ([Deng et al., CVPR 2009](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/5206848)) was published as a dataset paper. SQuAD ([Rajpurkar et al., EMNLP 2016](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.05250)) was published as a dataset paper. SWE-bench ([Jimenez et al., ICLR 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.06770)) was published as a benchmark paper. These are among the most-cited works in all of machine learning and natural language processing, not because they introduced clever algorithms, but because they *defined the problems* that clever algorithms would spend years solving.

This chapter guides you through the full picture: what D&B papers are, how they differ from Research papers and System Demo papers, what makes a strong contribution, and how to write one. Each section revisits Dr. Chen's dilemma to provide concrete, grounded examples. By the end, you will understand why her benchmark is indeed a separate paper, what it needs to contain, and how to frame it for the NeurIPS D&B track. You will also understand why the entire ML community has decided that data work deserves its own venue, and why that decision matters more than ever in an era of large language models, autonomous agents, and benchmark contamination.


### Chapter Introduction {#sec-chapter-intro}

To understand why Datasets & Benchmarks papers exist as a distinct category, you need to appreciate a fundamental asymmetry in how machine learning research has historically been valued. For the better part of two decades, prestige, citations, and career advancement in ML and NLP flowed through a single channel: algorithmic novelty. The incentive structure was clear. You took an existing benchmark (say, GLUE for natural language understanding, or ImageNet for image classification), proposed a new model, a new training procedure, or a new architectural modification, and showed that it achieved state-of-the-art results. The paper that *created* GLUE ([Wang et al., ICLR 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1804.07461)) was certainly cited, but it was cited as infrastructure, as something you used on the way to your real contribution: the model. The researchers who built GLUE, who designed the tasks, who curated the evaluation data, who built the leaderboard, who maintained the dataset over years? Their work was "service" work, not "research" work, in the eyes of the community.

This asymmetry had consequences. Dataset papers were difficult to publish because they did not fit the review criteria of algorithm-focused venues. Reviewers trained to ask "Where is the algorithmic novelty?" would judge a meticulous dataset curation effort by a standard it was never designed to meet. Benchmark papers fared slightly better. A new benchmark at least *defined* a task, which research culture recognized as valuable. However, even benchmark papers were often relegated to workshop papers or low-prestige venues. The people building the infrastructure on which the entire field depended were being systematically underrewarded for their work.

The turning point came in April 2021, when NeurIPS [announced the creation of a dedicated Datasets & Benchmarks track](https://neuripsconf.medium.com/announcing-the-neurips-2021-datasets-and-benchmarks-track-644e27c1e66c). The announcement was unusually blunt for an academic conference. It stated that work on datasets and benchmarks had been "undervalued, unsupported, and taken for granted"; strong language that acknowledged an institutional failure. The track aimed to make data work "first-class work on par with algorithms work," published in the main NeurIPS proceedings alongside research papers and given its own best-paper awards. The inaugural year received 484 submissions and accepted 174 papers. Among the early highlights were LAION-5B ([Schuhmann et al., NeurIPS 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.08402)), a dataset of 5.85 billion image-text pairs that would go on to enable Stable Diffusion, and MineDojo ([Fan et al., NeurIPS 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.08853)), a Minecraft-based benchmark for open-ended embodied AI that gave the reinforcement learning community an entirely new evaluation paradigm.

The growth since then has been striking. Submission numbers went from 484 in 2021 to 447 in 2022 (with integration into the main proceedings), then climbed rapidly to an estimated 900+ in 2023 and 1,820 in 2024: a nearly 4× increase from the inaugural year. The acceptance rate has remained competitive at approximately 36%, comparable to the main research track. Best-paper winners have included ClimSim ([Yu et al., NeurIPS 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.08754)), a dataset of 5.7 billion multivariate pairs for hybrid physics-ML climate emulation; DecodingTrust ([Wang et al., NeurIPS 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.11698)), a benchmark for evaluating GPT's trustworthiness across multiple safety dimensions; and PRISM ([Kirk et al., NeurIPS 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16019)), a participatory dataset spanning 75 countries for studying multicultural alignment in RLHF. These are not supplementary contributions. They are research artifacts that have shaped entire subfields.

The NeurIPS D&B track was a catalyst, not an endpoint. The broader research community has followed suit. In 2025, [KDD launched its own Datasets & Benchmarks track](https://kdd2025.kdd.org/call-for-datasets-and-benchmarks-track-papers/) for the first time, recognizing that data mining research also depends on high-quality evaluation infrastructure. The [Journal of Data-centric Machine Learning Research (DMLR)](https://dmlr.ai/), a new journal in the JMLR family, launched in October 2023 specifically to provide an archival home for data-focused ML research. Its inaugural volume included a paper titled "Building Better Datasets: Seven Recommendations," an explicit codification of what makes data work excellent. ACL, EMNLP, and NAACL do not have separate D&B tracks, but their reviewer guidelines now explicitly state that "development of datasets is as important as modeling work," and dataset resource papers are a recognized submission category within the main track. The [ACL Rolling Review (ARR) reviewer tutorial](https://aclrollingreview.org/reviewertutorial) makes a formal distinction between "artifact contributions" (datasets, systems, and tools: things you can download and use) and "knowledge contributions" (findings, theories, and algorithms: things you learn from reading). D&B papers are artifact contributions, and the review criteria reflect this.

So what, precisely, *is* a Datasets & Benchmarks paper? At its core, a D&B paper is a publication whose *primary contribution is a data artifact or evaluation infrastructure*, rather than a new algorithm, method, or theoretical result. The [NeurIPS 2025 call for papers](https://neurips.cc/Conferences/2025/CallForDatasetsBenchmarks) lays out the scope explicitly. Acceptable submissions include: new datasets; new benchmarks (with formal evaluation protocols, metrics, and baseline results); data generators and RL environments (such as simulation environments for training and testing agents); data-centric AI tools (for data labeling, curation, cleaning, and quality assessment); data curation practices (novel methodologies for collecting, annotating, or validating data); dataset audits (analyses of existing datasets for bias, quality, representativeness); and competition analyses (post-hoc analyses of machine learning challenge results). KDD's 2025 scope is similar, adding emphasis on data integration and temporal/spatial data. The unifying thread is that *the data or evaluation artifact is the star of the paper*, not a supporting actor.

This distinction is critical because it changes what reviewers look for. When a reviewer evaluates a research paper, they ask: "Does this advance the state of the art in terms of algorithmic performance, theoretical understanding, or empirical insight?" When a reviewer evaluates a D&B paper, they ask a different set of questions: "Is this dataset high-quality, well-documented, and accessible? Does this benchmark test something meaningful that existing benchmarks don't? Will the community use this? Is it ethically sourced and responsibly documented?" A dataset paper that introduces no new algorithm but provides the first large-scale, high-quality evaluation suite for a critical capability (say, multilingual reasoning in 40 languages) is a strong D&B contribution. A research paper that introduces a new algorithm and also releases a small dataset as a side contribution is a strong *research* contribution. The dataset is useful but ancillary. The venue should match the contribution.

The distinction extends to practical submission requirements. NeurIPS D&B papers are *single-blind*, meaning authors are visible to reviewers. This is a departure from the main track's double-blind policy. The rationale is that dataset and benchmark work often requires verifying that the data is actually hosted, accessible, and of the claimed quality, which is harder to do anonymously. Since 2025, NeurIPS requires all D&B submissions to include [Croissant](https://mlcommons.org/working-groups/data/croissant/) metadata (a machine-readable dataset description format supported by HuggingFace, Kaggle, OpenML, and Dataverse) and to host the dataset on a permanent platform. Papers that fail to provide accessible data at review time face desk rejection. This is a stricter enforcement than the main track, which still allows "code available upon request" in many cases.

For Dr. Chen, this picture is clarifying. Her multilingual reasoning benchmark (15,000 annotated questions across 40 languages, with a formal evaluation protocol, inter-annotator agreement metrics, and baseline experiments from frontier models) is precisely the kind of contribution the D&B track was created to value. It is not an appendix. It is not a footnote. It is a first-class research contribution that fills a specific gap in the evaluation infrastructure for multilingual AI. She will submit it to the NeurIPS D&B track, host it on HuggingFace with Croissant metadata, and write the paper with the data artifact at center stage. Meanwhile, her scoring algorithm (the novel metric that correlates better with human judgment) will go to the NeurIPS main track or to EMNLP, where reviewers will evaluate it on its algorithmic merits. Two contributions, two papers, two appropriate venues. Neither is diminished by the separation; both are strengthened.

The rest of this chapter walks through the details. @sec-track-comparison provides a thorough comparison of D&B papers, Research papers, and System Demo papers: what each track values, how review criteria differ, and how to decide which track is right for your work. @sec-anatomy-dataset dissects the canonical structure of a dataset paper, from the introduction to the ethics statement, with worked examples from best-paper winners. @sec-anatomy-benchmark does the same for benchmark papers, including Ofir Press's influential framework of three properties that every strong benchmark should have (natural, automatically evaluatable, challenging) and the pressing challenge of benchmark contamination. @sec-why-db-matters steps back to explain why D&B work has become more critical than ever in 2023–2026, driven by LLM benchmark saturation, agentic AI evaluation gaps, and the data-centric AI paradigm shift. Finally, @sec-how-to-write provides a practical guide to writing a competitive D&B submission, including submission logistics, writing tips, common rejection reasons, and a worked example of a complete submission package.

Throughout these sections, we return to Dr. Chen's journey. Each section applies its concepts to her multilingual reasoning benchmark, gradually transforming her initial dilemma into a concrete, well-structured submission. By the end, you will not only understand the D&B field; you will know how to work within it.


### Learning Objectives

After completing this chapter, you will be able to:

- **Distinguish** D&B papers from Research papers and System Demo papers in terms of what constitutes the primary contribution, how review criteria differ, and which venue is appropriate for which type of work
- **Identify** the landscape of venues that accept D&B work (NeurIPS D&B track, KDD D&B track, ACL/EMNLP main track resource papers, DMLR journal) and their specific requirements
- **Structure** a dataset paper using the canonical template: motivation, data collection methodology, documentation, baseline experiments, ethical considerations
- **Design** a benchmark following the three properties of a strong benchmark: natural tasks, automatic evaluability, and calibrated difficulty
- **Articulate** why D&B work is becoming more critical in the LLM and agentic AI era, including the evaluation crisis, benchmark contamination, and the data-centric AI paradigm
- **Prepare** a competitive D&B submission including the paper, hosted dataset, Croissant metadata, baseline code, and ethics statement

### Notation

This chapter is primarily conceptual and does not involve heavy mathematical notation. However, a few terms and abbreviations will appear repeatedly:

| Symbol / Abbreviation | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **D&B** | Datasets & Benchmarks (the track/paper type) | "The NeurIPS D&B track" |
| **κ** (kappa) | Cohen's kappa or Fleiss' kappa, inter-annotator agreement metrics | κ = 0.78 indicates "substantial agreement" |
| **α** (alpha) | Krippendorff's alpha, another inter-annotator agreement metric | α > 0.67 is typically the minimum for reliable annotation |
| **pass@k** | Probability that at least one of *k* generated code samples passes all test cases | pass@1 = 0.12 means 12% of single-attempt generations are correct |
| **IAA** | Inter-annotator agreement | "The IAA for our dataset was κ = 0.82" |
| ***CL venues** | ACL, EMNLP, NAACL, COLING, EACL (computational linguistics conferences) | "System demo papers at *CL venues" |
| **CFP** | Call for Papers | "Check the CFP for submission guidelines" |
